spec: MAdES — what the signing certificate asserts: the signer category (§a.11.2) and commitment constraints (§a.11.3)
generatedFrom: two certificates made with OpenSSL, self-signed with throwaway keys; recorded in reference/test/certpolicy.test.mjs from v1.9 until v1.10.1
note: Real DER certificates, because the risk in §a.11.3 is how ordinary certificates behave: they carry policy OIDs for reasons of their own, and a reader that takes those for constraints rejects every signature ever made. Nothing here trusts these certificates. Only their certificatePolicies extension is read; chain, validity and signature are out of scope. The expectations assume the reference assignments in `mapping`. A deployment with OIDs of its own gives its verifier its own mapping (§a.11.2, §a.11.3).
rules: Read certificatePolicies from the signing certificate itself, not from the issuer and not from the validated policy set of the path (§a.11.3 rule 1).
A certificate that asserts no category leaves the category asserted but not anchored: not invalid, and never human (§a.11.2).
Only OIDs in the mapping are constraints. A certificate asserting none of them is unconstrained, which is not the same as permitting nothing (§a.11.3 rule 2).
A certificate asserting one or more constraint OIDs permits exactly those commitments (§a.11.3 rule 3).
The commitment compared is the effective one: approval when the block has no commitment field (§a.11.3 rule 4, §a.4).
An unrecognised commitment exceeds any constraint; under an unconstrained certificate it stays an unrecognised commitment (§a.11.3 rule 5, §a.4).
A commitment that exceeds the constraint makes the signature invalid, and the report names the commitment and the permitted set (§a.5 step 9, §a.11.3 rule 6).

cases.name: a constrained machine credential
cases.note: Three policy OIDs: an assurance level under the same PEN that is neither a category nor a constraint, the category automated, and the single constraint creation. The absent commitment is the trap rule 4 closes: omitting the field claims approval, and this certificate does not permit it.

cases.name: an ordinary certificate whose policies are none of these
cases.note: The CA/Browser Forum domain-validated OID and an assurance level. It carries policies and none of them is a category or a constraint, so it asserts no category and is unconstrained. Read as constrained to the empty set, it would reject every commitment.

cases.name: bytes that do not parse as a certificate
cases.note: Three bytes of truncated DER. A reader that cannot read the certificate finds no category, so never human, and no constraint, so it does not reject a signature for its own limitation (§a.11, §a.5). What the signature itself comes to with such a certificate is a separate question and not pinned here.
